newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka troops build defences after rebel attack.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka troops build defences after rebel attack.

text.p: Sri Lankan troops, badly bruised in a daring attack by Tamil Tiger separatists in which more than 300 soldiers and rebels died, were busy patching their defences and regaining lost ground on Thursday, military officials said.

Military officials in the north said troops had patched a breach caused in the attack late on Tuesday and the main column of Operation "Jaya Sikuru", or "Sure of Victory", had linked up with the rear.
The operation is aimed at opening a key northern highway.
"The column linked up yesterday (Wednesday)," a Defence Ministry spokesman said on Thursday.
He said the situation in the area where the rebel attack occurred was under control and troops were consolidating their positions, He did not give further details.
More than 1,000 Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels attacked the army's artillery and mortar positions near Periyamadu, north of the government-held town of Vavuniya, late on Tuesday.
Vavuniya lies 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo.
Military officials said the rebels had punched a hole between half to one kilometre (quarter to half a mile) wide in the military's defence line.
Military officials in the north said 119 soldiers, including four officers, and 182 rebels were killed in the attack, which lasted five hours. Some 190 soldiers were wounded, they added.
The Defence Ministry said on Wednesday that four officers and 60 soldiers were killed and 68 were wounded in the attack. It said 150 rebels died in the battle and a large number were wounded.
But the clandestine Voice of Tiger radio, monitored in Vavuniya, on Thursday put the rebel death toll at 85, mostly women fighters.

The rebels, who are fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east, withdrew just before daybreak before troops could ask for air support to hit the enemy, military officials said.

Diplomats said the rebels were well placed to carry out such surprise attacks on the troops since the military was moving along a narrow strip, with the separatists controlling either side of the main highway.

"The LTTE did not make the same mistake as in the first attack at Thandikulam. They withdrew before daybreak and possibly saved themselves from more casualties which may have been caused once air force planes and helicopter gunships got into action," said an Asian diplomat.
"The LTTE will keep carrying out such attacks, but the military has to come up with a strategy to rush in reinforcement very quickly to beat the assaults," he added.

This was the second rebel attack in two weeks on troops involved in Operation Jaya Sikuru. The troops resumed their offensive through the brush jungles of the Wanni region on Monday to open a highway from Vavuniya to the Jaffna peninsula, a further 100 km (60 miles) north.
Two weeks ago, the rebels mounted a similar attack on the military's rear near Vavuniya, delaying the main offensive.
Official figures show that more than 300 government soldiers have been killed in the offensive since it was launched on May 13. The number of wounded is even higher.
Several hundred LTTE rebels are also reported to have been killed and wounded.
Independent confirmation of events is not possible as international media are not allowed in the battle zone.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the ethnic war, now in its 14th year. The LTTE say the toll is higher.
